the Guidelines for antibiotic therapy for prevention and treatment of infections in ICU patients have been updated, taking into account the most recent data on epidemiology, microbiology, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, clinical trials and cost effectiveness of antibiotic therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Guidelines are a useful instrument for physicians and microbiologists to provide optimal treatment for ICU infections, and to reduce hospital-acquired infections and their associated mortality.

the use of antibiotic therapy in the ICU should be guided by: (i) knowledge of epidemiological patterns of hospital infections; (ii) knowledge of the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic parameters for the antibiotic(s) chosen for the patient; (iii) knowledge of the concentration of the antibiotic at the site of infection.
we have developed a series of recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of nosocomial infections in ICUs, which will be of use to clinicians in their day-to-day practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, despite the fact that there are a number of guidelines on antimicrobial chemotherapy for ICU infections available, they are not always up to date and they do not always take into account the most recent data from clinical trials.
the guidelines are not only a tool for the clinician but also a tool for the hospital administration to implement the best practices in the management of infections in the intensive care unit.

, in order to achieve optimal results, antibiotic therapy should be based on: (1) proper identification of the infection site; (2) local surveillance of the most frequent nosocomial microorganisms; (3) identification of the environmental risk factors and of the underlying condition of the patient; (4) microbiological diagnosis, when possible.
